title: What happens to a pipeline when one consumer lags (consumer-group lag, partition rebalancing, back-pressure), and how do you keep the pipeline healthy (scaling consumers, monitoring lag, dead-letter queues for poison records)?
shortTitle: Consumer lag, rebalancing, back-pressure, and keeping a pipeline healthy

s1_definition.profdef: Consumer lag is the gap between the latest offset produced to a partition and the offset a consumer group has committed, meaning unprocessed backlog. When a consumer is added, removed, or dies, the group rebalances, reassigning partitions among the remaining consumers. Back-pressure is the mechanism by which a slow downstream stage signals upstream to slow down so buffers do not overflow. A pipeline is kept healthy by scaling consumers up to the partition count, monitoring lag and error rates, handling back-pressure, and routing poison records to a dead-letter queue.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the National Bank of India's transaction counter where slips arrive on a conveyor (Kafka). Consumer lag is the growing pile of unprocessed slips when the clerk is too slow. If a clerk goes on break, the remaining clerks reshuffle who handles which tray — that reshuffle is a rebalance, and during it processing briefly pauses. Back-pressure is the slow clerk telling the conveyor "stop feeding me, I'm swamped" so slips do not spill on the floor. You keep the counter healthy by adding clerks up to the number of trays, watching the pile size, and when one slip is so garbled it keeps jamming the machine, you set it aside in a special reject tray (dead-letter queue) so the rest keep flowing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Lag is unprocessed backlog; rebalancing redistributes partitions; back-pressure slows producers; and you stay healthy by scaling consumers, monitoring lag, and dead-lettering poison records.

sections.s2_technical:
Consumer lag is the most important health signal for a streaming pipeline. Each partition has a log-end offset, the newest message, and each consumer group commits the offset it has processed. Lag is the difference. Small, stable lag is fine; steadily growing lag means the consumer cannot keep up and the pipeline is falling behind, which in a bank could mean fraud alerts arriving minutes late. You read lag per partition and per group, and it is the first thing to alert on. The cause is usually that processing per message is too slow, there are too few consumers, or a downstream dependency is slow.

Partition rebalancing happens whenever group membership changes — a consumer joins, leaves, or is considered dead after missing heartbeats. The group coordinator reassigns partitions so each live consumer owns a share. During a naive rebalance, a stop-the-world pause occurs where no one consumes, which briefly spikes lag, and in-flight work can be reprocessed, which is why idempotency matters. Modern cooperative or incremental rebalancing reduces the pause by only moving the partitions that must move. A key constraint is that within a group a partition is owned by exactly one consumer, so you cannot have more active consumers than partitions; extra consumers sit idle. That is why partition count sets your maximum parallelism.

Back-pressure is how a pipeline protects itself from overload. If a downstream stage like a database write is slower than ingestion, an unbounded buffer would grow until memory is exhausted. Back-pressure propagates the slowness upstream: in a pull-based consumer you simply poll less, and in frameworks like Flink or reactive streams the slow operator signals the fast one to emit less. The effect is that the whole pipeline runs at the speed of its slowest stage rather than crashing. You tune this by bounding queues, setting fetch sizes, and sometimes load-shedding non-critical work.

Keeping the pipeline healthy combines several practices. You scale consumers horizontally up to the partition count, and if you need more parallelism you increase partitions. You monitor lag, throughput, processing latency, and per-stage error rate, and alert when lag grows or errors spike. You make processing idempotent so a rebalance's reprocessing does no harm. And you handle poison records — a malformed message that keeps failing — by retrying a bounded number of times and then routing it to a dead-letter queue, a separate topic, so one bad message never blocks its partition forever. A senior nuance is to monitor the dead-letter queue itself, because a rising DLQ rate signals an upstream data-quality problem, and in a bank you attach clear ownership and alerting so a poison transaction is investigated rather than silently discarded.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A slow consumer falls behind and the backlog grows. This is exactly consumer lag — measure produced minus processed offsets.

Problem 2 — One malformed transaction keeps failing and would block its partition. This is exactly a dead-letter queue — retry, then divert.

Problem 3 — Adding a consumer must redistribute partitions. This is exactly a rebalance — reassign partitions across the group.

The mini-project simulates a consumer group. `PartitionLog` holds produced messages with offsets. `ConsumerGroup` assigns partitions to consumers, processes messages while committing offsets, computes lag, retries poison records up to a limit then sends them to a dead-letter queue, and rebalances when a consumer is added. The demo produces messages including a poison record, processes with lag measurement, dead-letters the poison record, and rebalances after adding a consumer.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four messages on partition zero: offsets 0 and 1 valid, offset 2 a poison record with a null amount, and offset 3 valid.

Step 1 — Consumer joins, rebalance. Consumer-A joins the group and is assigned partition zero. The rebalance log notes the assignment across the group, which is how Kafka distributes work.

Step 2 — Poll and process. Consumer-A reads from the committed offset forward. Offsets 0 and 1 process successfully and their progress is committed, so lag shrinks as each is handled.

Step 3 — Poison record. Offset 2 has a null amount, so processing fails. The consumer retries up to the limit of three, each attempt failing, then diverts the message to the dead-letter queue and commits past it so the partition is not blocked.

Step 4 — Continue past poison. Offset 3 processes successfully, proving that one poison record did not stall the whole partition. After the poll, the committed offset equals the log-end offset, so lag is zero.

Step 5 — Add consumer, rebalance again. Consumer-B joins, triggering another rebalance that redistributes partitions across the two consumers. The dead-letter queue holds the one poison record for later investigation, and the pipeline stayed healthy throughout.

```
INFO: REBALANCE: consumer consumer-A joined; reassigning 1 partitions across 1 consumers
INFO: === POLL (process, measure lag, DLQ poison) ===
WARNING: retry 1 failed for offset 2
WARNING: retry 2 failed for offset 2
WARNING: retry 3 failed for offset 2
WARNING: DLQ: poison record at offset 2 diverted
INFO: Partition 0 lag now = 0
INFO: DLQ size = 1
INFO: === Add a consumer → rebalance ===
INFO: REBALANCE: consumer consumer-B joined; reassigning 1 partitions across 2 consumers
```

  Producers → Partition 0: [off0 ok][off1 ok][off2 POISON][off3 ok]
                              │
                              ▼ consumer-A polls from committed offset
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Consumer Group (txn-processors)                │
  │  process off0 commit                         │

  │  process off2 retry×3 → DLQ, commit past it  │

sections.s6_takeaway:
Consumer lag is the single most important health signal for a streaming pipeline. Each partition has a newest offset, each consumer group commits the offset it has processed, and lag is the difference, meaning the unprocessed backlog. Small stable lag is fine, but steadily growing lag means the consumer cannot keep up and the pipeline is falling behind, which in a bank could make fraud alerts arrive minutes late, so lag is the first thing I alert on. The usual causes are slow per-message processing, too few consumers, or a slow downstream dependency.

Partition rebalancing happens whenever group membership changes, when a consumer joins, leaves, or dies after missing heartbeats, and the coordinator reassigns partitions so each live consumer owns a share. A naive rebalance causes a brief stop-the-world pause that spikes lag and can reprocess in-flight work, which is why idempotency matters, and cooperative incremental rebalancing reduces that pause. A hard constraint is that within a group a partition is owned by exactly one consumer, so you cannot have more active consumers than partitions, which means partition count sets your maximum parallelism. Back-pressure is how the pipeline protects itself when a downstream stage is slower than ingestion, propagating the slowness upstream so the whole pipeline runs at the speed of its slowest stage instead of exhausting memory and crashing.

To keep the pipeline healthy I scale consumers horizontally up to the partition count and add partitions when I need more parallelism, I monitor lag, throughput, latency, and per-stage error rate with alerts, I make processing idempotent so a rebalance does no harm, and I handle poison records by retrying a bounded number of times and then routing them to a dead-letter queue so one bad message never blocks its partition. I also monitor the dead-letter queue itself, because a rising DLQ rate points to an upstream data-quality problem.

In my project at the National Bank of India this is exactly how the transaction consumer group ran. When a malformed transaction with a null amount kept failing, the consumer retried it a few times and then diverted it to a dead-letter queue, committing past it so the rest of the partition kept flowing, and when we added a consumer the group rebalanced to share the partitions. We watched consumer-group lag closely and attached clear ownership and alerting to the dead-letter queue, because in a bank a poison transaction must be investigated rather than silently dropped.
